• The lamp had to be lit at dusk, every dusk, and this was the first thing anyone learned about the job. Thomas Marlowe had learned it from his
  father, who had learned it from a man named Croft, who had kept the light before anyone alive could remember. The tower stood on a rock called
  Harrow Point, three miles off the coast, close enough to the mainland to see the trees on a clear day and far enough that no one came unless they
  meant to. The light flashed every ten seconds. It had flashed every ten seconds for one hundred and thirty years. Thomas could lie in his bunk at
  night and count the flashes the way other men counted sheep.

  He was fifty-eight. He had been on the rock for thirty-one years, first as an assistant, then alone. His wife had lived out there with him for six
  of them, until she stopped sleeping through the foghorns and started taking the boat to town more often, and then one day she took the boat and did
  not come back. There was no anger in it. She wrote to him from her sister's house, said she was sorry, said the rock was no place to grow old. He
  read the letter twice, put it in the drawer with the tide tables, and lit the lamp at dusk as usual. That was the year he stopped thinking of the
  mainland as a place he might retire to and started thinking of it as a place he could see.

He did not know that night that anything had been out there. He learned it three days later, when the supply boat brought the coastguard's letter. A
  fishing boat called the Grace Maguire, out of the harbor forty miles south, had been running home through the storm, and her master had seen the
  light go dark at the exact moment he had been using it to check his distance off the point. He had turned away — seaward, into the weather — and
  held off until the light showed again, and then stood in and passed the rock at a safe distance and got home. His letter said, in the flat way men
  wrote such things: Your nine minutes were noticed. The margin was not wide. Thomas read it at the kitchen table with the letter from his wife in the
  same drawer, and then he went up the tower and checked the driving wire, and the next week he replaced it, and every month after that for the rest
  of his time on the rock he checked it again, whether the log required it or not.

  The years after that were quieter. The engines were replaced by an electric compressor, and the kerosene lamp by an electric lamp, and the clockwork
  by a motor, and each change made the work easier and took something from it that he could not name. There was less to fix and therefore less to
  know. He found he missed the smell of the kerosene. He began, without deciding to, to write longer entries in the log — small things, a seal pup on
  the landing stage in March, the first puffins in April, ice on the handrail of the north gallery, a rainbow that ended in the sea so exactly it
  looked moored there. Some inspector years later would call these entries irregular. Thomas thought of them as the true record, more than the
  barometer readings, and he was probably right.

  The letter from the Board came when he was sixty. It said the light was to be automated. It said the automation was reliable. It said the keeper
  could be accommodated ashore with a pension, and thanked him for his service. He read it standing at the window, and then he sat down and read it
  again, and then he went out and split wood for two hours though he had wood enough for the whole winter. What he could not explain to the Board, and
  did not try, was that the light was not a machine to him. It was a promise he had made on behalf of strangers, renewed every ten seconds, every
  night, for thirty-one years, and a promise is not the same thing when no one is there to keep it.

  The automation crew came in October. They were polite young men with instruments, and they did their work in four days, and on the last evening they
  asked if he wanted to light the lamp himself one final time. He said he did not, because the electric light did not need lighting, only switching,
  and it would have been a ceremony about a thing that had none. Instead he climbed the tower alone at dusk and stood in the lantern room while the
  automatic system took over, the motor turning the lens with a hum very like the old clockwork's, the beam sweeping out over the water every ten
  seconds as it had always done. He watched it for one full hour. Then he went down the ninety-three steps, counted them as he always did, and packed
  his bag.

  He took the ferry in the morning. Passing the point, he looked back and saw the tower white in the sun, the lens turning inside it, doing its work
  without him, and he found that this was all right. The promise did not belong to him. It belonged to whoever was out there in the dark, and as long
  as the light flashed, the promise was being kept, by whatever hands. He turned his face to the mainland and did not look back again, and that
  evening, in his sister's house, with a real fire and a carpet and the sound of traffic in the street, he lay awake for a while at dusk, out of
  habit, and counted — though there was nothing to count — and slept.
